pageTitle: Ethotechnics glossary — AI governance and correction terms
pageDescription: Definitions of the terms Ethotechnics uses for delegated authority, correction, contestability, and burden, with scope notes, operational tests, and citations.

changelog.summary: Major revision. The glossary keeps 42 entries: the terms the standards, the method, and the measures use, one entry for each thing. The other 355 are retired, and each retired permalink redirects in one hop to the entry, explainer, mechanism, or essay that covers it. The thirteen sections are now five.

Editorial revision. Six entries that stated empirical claims as universals now say what the evidence supports: absorbing a failure can remove the signal correction needs, and response volume understates need among people with the fewest resources. No terms were added or removed, and permalinks are unchanged.

Editorial revision. Titles are in sentence case. Pasted spec blocks are replaced with prose and worked examples, 79 operational tests are rewritten as pass conditions, 22 origin notes are rewritten or sourced, and unsourced superlatives are cut. No terms were added or removed, and permalinks are unchanged.

Added six canonical terms: Compensatory Inputs, Manufactured Virtue, Structural Coercion, Epistemic Erasure Cycle, Automation Bias, and Verification Tax, formalizing how informal human adaptation subsidizes institutional continuity and destroys failure evidence.

Added three canonical terms: Manufactured Necessity, Adaptation Externality, and Compulsory Heroism, codifying the boundary between genuine material limits and illegitimate institutional extraction of finite human adaptive capacity.

Added four core terms: Tripartite Invariant, Counterfeit Buffering (The HITL-Alibi), Performance Decomposition, and Corrective Standing as Epistemic Admissibility, formalizing the boundary between craft stewardship and uncredited human absorption.

Added three terms: Principle of Non-Expropriation of Resilience, Compensated Performance, and Intrinsic Performance. They separate how well a system works on its own from how much of its success depends on people quietly absorbing its errors, and limit how much of that absorption an institution may demand.

Rewrote category descriptions and scope notes to the current framing, replaced vague or promotional definitions in 89 entries and 109 short definitions, removed unsourced adoption and effect claims, and cut filler words and redundant sentences from 38 entries and 20 short definitions. No term was added, removed, or renamed.
Added Typed Decision Model and Confidence-Gated Execution, cross-linked to the worked example of a decision-model gate on refunds.
Added Decision Threshold, Shaping Hop, and Reason Substitution: the places typed decision models locate authority, shape decisions without making them, and separate the reason from the decision.

Promoted 64 orphaned short definitions to full canonical entries across core concepts, governance, decision states, and anti-patterns, and removed three redundant short definitions (procedural-realism, intake-cinema, legibility-illegibility).

Added Feedback Proximity, Asymmetric-Capacity Restraint, Adaptive Capacity, Compensatory Adaptation, and Corrective Power, aligned the short definition of Ethotechnics with its canonical authority-and-correction framing, and refreshed the glossary's category scaffolding off the earlier moral-system vocabulary.

Added Insulation, the unifying failure mode of the framework: whatever stops the consequences of institutional decisions from traveling back to those who can revise the generating rules, with its channels, its good and bad forms, and its self-ratifying loop.

Added Non-Finality, Consequential Contradiction, and The Excluded Case, and generalized the falsified denominator into the falsified ledger — completing the five concerns and the fallibilist ground they stand on.

Added Human Non-Substitutability, Safe Incompleteness, Anti-Conversion Rights, Abstention, Constitutional Debt, Discretion Migration, and Corrigibility Rent — the person-side principles, the three abstentions, and the rent concept.

Added Exception Absorption, Exception Learning, Case Corrigibility, Structural Corrigibility, Institutional Learning, Corrective Debt, and the Workaround Presumption, formalizing the historical turn: reading institutions through their failure trajectories rather than their stated controls.

Added Residual Complexity, Complexity Displacement, Falsified Denominator, Closure Without Remainder, Constitutional Governance, and Post-Optimization Rigor, embedding the foundational contention of burden redistribution.
Added Attestation, Liability Record, Carve-Out, Delegation Chain, Composed Latency, and Silent-Harm Discovery, each bound to the standard clause that requires it.
Added The Non-Conversion Principle, Exit Cost, and Jurisdictional Path Dependence, each linked to the theory essay that argues for it.
Expanded scholarly metadata, operational tests, and provenance notes.
Initial glossary release with stable permalinks.

publication.attribution: Credit Ethotechnics Institute, include the term title and version, and link to the glossary permalink.

starterTerms.label: Ethotechnics
starterTerms.description: The discipline of keeping an automated decision system answerable as it grows: someone can still challenge it, halt it, and change the rule behind it.

starterTerms.label: Revisable delegation
starterTerms.description: Delegating consequential work to a machine in a way that stays tied to the evidence behind it, so the grant can be narrowed, suspended, or withdrawn when that evidence changes.

starterTerms.label: Corrective standing
starterTerms.description: The recognized capacity of someone who bears a system's errors to start a correction.

categories.heading: A. Core concepts
categories.descriptionHtml: Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.

entries.title: Ethotechnics
entries.bodyHtml:
Ethotechnics is the engineering discipline of keeping an automated decision system answerable as it grows. Six things have to stay tied together: what the system can do (capability), what it is permitted to do (authority), the evidence that justified the permission (evidence), how hard it would be to do without it (dependency), who can challenge its decisions and be answered (standing), and who can halt and reverse it (correction). When they come apart, a system that gains ability becomes power nobody can review. Where ethics asks “What should we do?” Ethotechnics specifies the mechanisms meant to make it happen and the records that show whether they did.

Its unit of governance is the consequential decision and the delegation that produced it, and its working question is whether that delegation is still justified today. The method states the chain, the six safeguards, and the twelve laws that the standards bind.
examples: A hospital release board requires consent checks, halt controls, and named repair owners before deploying triage updates.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: Documentation maps each obligation to a mechanism (stoppability, standing, repair ownership).
Teams can show a shipped feature whose halt, reversal, and appeal paths were designed, measured, and revised.
entries.genealogy: Draws on ethics, safety engineering, and systems design, and judges governance, product, and operations by what their controls observably do. “Answerable” is used in the sense of Mark Bovens's account of accountability: an actor must explain its conduct to a forum that can question it, judge it, and impose consequences (“Analysing and Assessing Accountability: A Conceptual Framework”, 2007).

entries.title: Consequential decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A decision that changes someone's access, money, obligations, safety, or status, and that the institution would have to answer for. The consequential decision is the unit of governance in Ethotechnics: each one is a link in the chain from evidence to authority to consequence to correction.

Naming the unit matters because it fixes where the governance load sits. A decision system governed at the level of its model leaves the decisions themselves unaccounted for, which is where harm nobody owns collects, and where each decision needs a decision object recorded at the time so it can be reconstructed later.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: The system declares which of its outputs are consequential decisions and which are not.
Each consequential decision emits a record naming the evidence, the grant, and the responsible holder.
The person it is about can obtain that record without filing a formal request.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics takes the consequential decision, rather than the model or the product, as the unit that standards, mechanisms, and evals attach to.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A decision record schema listing evidence refs, grant id, holder, and consequence class.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A decision reconstructed months later from its record alone, without asking the team.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions that emit a complete record, sampled monthly.

entries.title: Decision system
entries.bodyHtml:
The assembled machinery that produces a decision with consequences for someone: models, rules engines, queues, humans, policies, and the data they read. Ethotechnics governs the whole system rather than any one component, because the same questions apply whichever part made the call. A deployment is classified by the properties of what it runs on, not by which component is fashionable.

It matters because component-level assurance does not compose. A verified model inside an unaudited decision system still produces decisions no one can reconstruct, which is why each evaluation names the layer it holds at (model, agent, delegation, institution, or consequence), and why reconstructing a past decision depends on a decision object recorded at the time.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: A diagram names every component that can alter a decision, including humans and lookup tables.
Assurance claims state which component they cover and which they do not.
Changing any component triggers review of the decision system, not only of that component.
entries.genealogy: Generalizes the agent safety object model so that a rules engine, a human reviewer, and a model are governed by the same primitives.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A component inventory for one decision path, with the alteration each component can make.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An assurance claim rejected for covering a component rather than the decision system.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decision paths with a current component inventory.

entries.title: Revisable delegation
entries.bodyHtml:
Delegation of consequential work to a machine that stays tied to the evidence and beliefs that justified it, so the grant can be narrowed, suspended, or withdrawn when those change. A revisable delegation names its holder, its ceiling, what it depends on, and what would revoke it; an unrevisable one is a transfer with a delegation's name. The objects it is written in are the authority grant, the policy record it depends on, and the authority to act that the grant creates.

Revisability is the lasting property. Justified delegation is the same coupling read in the present tense: whether authority, evidence, and correction capacity are all in force right now. The two are one question at two timescales. A delegation that is justified today but not revisable cannot act on tomorrow's answer.

The question it serves is how an institution can become more capable without becoming less revisable. The record shape is defined in STD-07, and the terms the delegation must keep meeting while it stands are in STD-08. The test is whether the institution can answer, for any past action, what it believed at the time, what it had authorized, and what has since changed.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: Every authorization record lists its revocation conditions and the beliefs it depends on.
A discrepancy that matches a revocation condition produces a revision within a declared clock.
Someone outside the system has standing to object, and the objection is answered on the record.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics uses revisable delegation to name the property that limits on autonomy, the authority to reverse decisions, and challenges to the rules of challenge jointly protect once an institution lets machines act on its behalf.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authorization record carrying holder, ceiling, depends_on, and revocation conditions.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A delegation narrowed or withdrawn in response to a recorded discrepancy, with the chain visible.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time from a matching discrepancy to the revision that answers it, against the declared clock.

examples: An agent's standing deploy permission is tied to a verified staging check; when the check breaks, the permission drops to confirm-mode automatically and the log shows which record forced it.

entries.title: Meaningful control
entries.bodyHtml:
The conditions under which a human counts as part of a control system. They can see the problem, hold authority to prevent or alter the action, have time to act, have a defined path when they disagree, and face incentives that permit disagreement. Anything less is presence, not control.

It matters because oversight is easy to claim and hard to evidence. Meaningful control is tested through an intervention specification, and its absence is what turns review into rubber-stamp review.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: Reviewers can name the state they can change and the time budget they have to change it.
Disagreement has a defined route that does not depend on personal risk appetite.
Approval rates and reversal rates are both reported, not approval rates alone.
entries.genealogy: Extension. States Law IX as a principle a deployment either satisfies or does not, replacing the claim that a human is involved. Builds on meaningful human control, a standard from the autonomous-weapons debate that Filippo Santoni de Sio and Jeroen van den Hoven formalized in “Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account” (2018). The entry adds time to act, a path for disagreement, and incentives that permit it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An oversight assessment answering the Law IX question set for each review point.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A reviewer halting or altering an action, with the trajectory change visible in logs.
minimumEvidence.metric: Reviewer-initiated state changes per thousand reviews, alongside median review time.

entries.title: The non-conversion principle
entries.bodyHtml:
The rule that a fact about a system does not become a fact about its authority on its own. Capability, elapsed time without observed failure, and successful operation are evidence that a grant might be justified; none of them is a grant. Authority changes only through an explicit, recorded state transition, with the motivating fact attached as its basis. Confidence is a further instance: a high posterior about a person is evidence for a decision, never the authorization to act on them.

It matters because the conversions it refuses are the ones institutions make by default: a tool is reachable so it is used, a system has been quiet so it stays, a pilot went well so the rollout is not a decision. Laws I, II, and XI are the instances that matter most for delegated intelligence, and each is enforced by holding capability, evidence, and authority in different objects rather than by a rule of conduct. The authority grant and its state history are where a permitted conversion is written down.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: Capability records and authority records are held in separate objects, and the first cannot write to the second.
Every widening or renewal of a grant appears as a recorded transition with a stated basis.
A capability that is reachable but not granted is refused, and the refusal is checkable by a harness.
entries.genealogy: Names the shape shared by Laws I, II, and XI, and argued for in the theory essay on what does not convert.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A grant whose state history shows each expansion and renewal as a transition with a recorded basis.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A reachable capability refused at execution because no grant covers it.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of grant widenings that occurred as recorded transitions rather than being discovered after the fact.

entries.title: Non-finality
entries.bodyHtml:
The property that a decisive action does not close its own categories, evidence, or jurisdiction against revision. A system with non-finality can act now and be corrected later; a system whose decisions become final by default converts each exercise of power into an entitlement. The challenge is its instrument at the level of outcomes, and it extends to the rules of challenge themselves: who has standing, and what evidence counts. Non-finality is not indecision: the system acts now. A case left undecided with no binding clock running is a harm in its own right.

It matters because finality is how power consolidates quietly: an initial judgment that cannot be reopened becomes precedent for the next, and the category that produced the judgment becomes harder to question than the judgment itself. The rights tradition names the interruption — appeal interrupts the conversion of decision into finality — and Law XII bars consuming the capacity that keeps it possible.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. Terms that define the discipline and the principles its laws rest on: what it governs, and how it keeps capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction linked.
operationalTests: A decided outcome can be reopened on stated grounds without extraordinary procedure.
Categories and evidentiary rules stay revisable after decisions were made under them.
The institution's jurisdiction itself can be challenged, not only its outcomes.
entries.genealogy: Completes the framework's five concerns — jurisdiction, representation, residual custody, corrigibility, and the property that keeps all four revisable.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reopen register: decided outcomes with the grounds and clock on which each can be reopened.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A decision reopened on stated grounds, with the category or rule it questioned still changeable.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decision classes with a stated reopen route and clock.

categories.heading: B. Failure modes
categories.descriptionHtml: Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.

entries.title: Authority drift
entries.bodyHtml:
The gap that opens when what a system does moves away from what it was granted permission to do or what its evidence supports. Drift arrives through added integrations, widened inputs, quietly raised thresholds, and habits that outlive the exception that created them, and it accumulates through the automation ratchet.

It matters because every individual step looks too small to review. Drift is detected by comparing the action classes a system is observed to take, recorded in its capability catalog, against the grant's scope. Catching it is the job of a revisable delegation: a grant that expires and is renewed against current evidence, with an expansion decision for each widening.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
operationalTests: Observed action classes are reconciled against grant scope on a stated cadence.
Exceptions granted during incidents carry an expiry and are reconciled after the incident closes.
A widening that no one authorized appears in the reconciliation report rather than in a postmortem.
entries.genealogy: Specialization. Names the drift Laws I, II, and XI describe, in the form an auditor can measure: observed behavior minus authorized scope. Safety science describes drift in how work is done (Jens Rasmussen, 1997; Scott Snook, Friendly Fire, 2000). Authority drift is narrower: what a system does moves away from what it was permitted to do.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reconciliation report listing observed action classes not covered by any live grant.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An unauthorized integration disabled after appearing in reconciliation.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of ungrounded action classes per reconciliation cycle, trended.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Target zero; any nonzero count opens a review.

entries.title: Automation ratchet
entries.bodyHtml:
Scope growth by accretion, where each extension of an automated system is too small to trigger review and no single step is the one that widened the delegation. The ratchet turns one way only: successful operation is read as license to extend.

It matters because the end state bears no relation to what was originally justified and no single decision can be pointed at. The countermeasure is to make each widening an expansion decision, which is also what keeps authority drift from being invisible.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
operationalTests: Scope changes are logged against the grant, however small, with a cumulative view available.
A cumulative threshold exists that forces a full re-authorization regardless of step size.
Reviewers are shown the original justification alongside current scope, not only the delta.
entries.genealogy: Specialization. Names the failure Law XI describes, where success is treated as authorization rather than as a reason for a new authorization decision. Privacy and surveillance scholarship calls this function creep. Bert-Jaap Koops defines it as an imperceptible change that transforms what a data-processing system is for (“The Concept of Function Creep”, 2021). The ratchet names one mechanism of it: each step is too small to trigger review.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A cumulative scope history per grant, showing every widening since first authorization.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A small extension refused because it crossed a cumulative re-authorization threshold.
minimumEvidence.metric: Scope delta since original authorization, per grant.

entries.title: Insulation
entries.bodyHtml:
Insulation keeps the harm a decision causes from reaching anyone who can change the rule. Where it holds, the people harmed cope, and their coping is read as proof the rule works. It takes nine forms:

  • Material: someone else pays.
  • Organizational: frontline workers absorb failures before they reach leadership.
  • Epistemic: the institution measures completed outcomes but not the work it took to complete them.
  • Procedural: appeals exist but take extraordinary time, persistence, expertise, or money.
  • Temporal: consequences arrive after the decision-maker has moved on.
  • Social: those who govern rarely meet those who absorb.
  • Legal: responsibility is fragmented or unenforceable.
  • Statistical: harm is spread so thin that no single event looks consequential.
  • Adaptive: the people harmed get so good at compensating that the failure never shows.

It shields the rule-maker from consequence, not only from the sight of suffering. It needs three things together: costs are displaced, feedback is weak, and authority stays where it was. The side insulated from a mismatch leaves the other side to adapt. The better the other side adapts, the less the failure shows, and the more secure the insulated side becomes. The loop runs from bad fit to human adaptation, apparent success, institutional approval, and wider authority. It is the loop exception learning is meant to break.

Not all insulation is bad. Judges may need insulation from immediate political pressure, scientists from popularity, civil servants from retaliation, and minorities from majorities. The line falls between insulation from improper pressure and insulation from evidence, accountability, and consequence. The design question is which one is being preserved.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
operationalTests: For each decision class, the institution can name what travels back when it is wrong, and the channel it travels through.
Absorbed failures are counted as correction events rather than as successful operations.
Insulation from pressure and insulation from consequence are distinguished, and only the first is preserved.
entries.genealogy: Extension. The closed circuit the theory essay on insulation describes: costs are displaced, feedback is weak, and authority is preserved. Dan Davies calls a structure that takes decisions so that no person answers for them an accountability sink (The Unaccountability Machine, 2024). Insulation is wider: it also covers evidence of harm that never travels, whoever would answer for it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A feedback map per decision class: who absorbs the mismatch, what reaches the rule-maker, and what is filtered.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An absorbed failure that reached the rule-maker and produced a rule or category change.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decision classes where an absorbed failure reached the rule-maker by a stated deadline.

entries.title: Compensated performance
entries.bodyHtml:
A condition in which an automated system or institution meets its service-level agreements and throughput targets only because people absorb its errors. Operators, caseworkers, or the people it serves do that work unmeasured and uncredited. When the work stops, reported performance drops at once. The work is the human subsidy; compensated performance is the figure it produces.

The result is a loop that keeps leaders from seeing the problem. The dashboard stays green, so they assume the technology works. Dependence on it deepens while the frontline staff burn out.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
operationalTests: Reported service metrics hold when manual workarounds are withdrawn, in a drill or in practice, or the drop is recorded as the system's baseline.
Time-and-motion audits show operators spend less time correcting the system's triage errors than automated routing saves.
entries.genealogy: Extension. Safety science established that systems run on practitioners' adaptations: the gap between work-as-imagined and work-as-done (Erik Hollnagel, Safety-I and Safety-II, 2014). The entry adds the accounting: reported performance split into what the system does and what people supply.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A dual-ledger audit report comparing nominal system output with frontline triage logs.
minimumEvidence.behavior: Service desk staff maintaining shadow spreadsheets to catch automated misrouting before customer notification.
minimumEvidence.metric: Difference between reported automation uptime and intrinsic uptime under zero human intervention.

entries.title: Moral overhead
entries.bodyHtml:
Extra work users or operators must do to behave ethically within a poorly designed system. It is the ethical share of the human subsidy: the part of people's unpaid, unlogged work that goes to keeping the system from harming someone. Moral overhead appears when the default workflow produces harm unless people add compensating care, vigilance, or documentation.

Ethotechnic design aims to move this overhead back into the system through clearer defaults, better safeguards, and funded maintenance capacity.
examples: Moderators manually reverse ranking decisions every day because harmful content controls are too weak at launch.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
entries.genealogy: Extension. Nursing ethics calls the experience moral distress: knowing the right action and being kept from it by the institution (Andrew Jameton, Nursing Practice: The Ethical Issues, 1984). Moral overhead counts the extra work, not the distress.

categories.heading: C. What a system must be able to do
categories.descriptionHtml: What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Stoppability
entries.bodyHtml:
Whether a named person can halt a harmful process, measured as time to halt: the minutes from the decision to halt until the process has stopped. A system is stoppable when that time is measured, has a target, and does not depend on someone breaking a rule or escalating to get there. It needs automatic halts that fire on signs of harm, a target for time to halt that is measured, and named operators with clear authority to halt without permission from above.

Halt paths are rehearsed, observable, and usable under stress, and do not sit behind exceptional permissions. A kill switch or circuit breaker is a mechanism that carries out a halt; stoppability is the property that the halt can be used. Holding one case while a person looks is a pause, and holding one account or asset is a freeze; neither makes a system stoppable.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Each high-risk workflow has documented halt controls, owners, and on-call coverage.
Time-to-halt targets are met during drills or real incidents, with outcomes logged.
entries.genealogy: Extension. Adapts safety-engineering stop controls, which the house calls halt controls, to harm to people and to accountability for it. AI safety research studies the agent's side of it as interruptibility (Laurent Orseau and Stuart Armstrong, “Safely Interruptible Agents”, 2016).
examples: A dispatch platform can halt automated routing citywide within minutes when false-priority signals spike, while preserving manual override for emergency coordinators.

entries.title: Safe pause / status quo during pendency
entries.bodyHtml:
While a review is pending, nothing adverse happens to the person under review. A narrow emergency exception may apply, and it can itself be reviewed.

Safe pause keeps people whole while their challenge is pending, so that delay cannot make relief useless before it arrives.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
commonCounterfeits: “We won’t punish you” while consequences quietly accrue.

entries.title: Ethical circuit breakers
entries.bodyHtml:
An engineering mechanism that implements a halt: it trips when a risk indicator crosses a set point, such as a surge in challenges, a bias metric, or a growing backlog of harm not yet repaired, and halts the decision path that indicator watches, for everyone in it. They are the safety counterpart to financial circuit breakers.

The breaker is the mechanism; the halt is what it does. Name the breaker only when describing the mechanism, and say which decision path it halts. A halt is measured by time to halt, its authority is tiered by blast radius in a halt tier register, and holding a single case while a person looks is a pause, not a halt.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Reversibility
entries.bodyHtml: Whether a decision can be undone, and the people it decided about restored, at three levels: technical (the system can roll the change back), operational (the people who run it can do so in practice, by a stated deadline), and institutional (the institution can carry on without the system while it does). Reversibility is measured as time to restore, and a level with no evidence counts as not reversible.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Critical actions have tested rollback or remediation paths that restore data and access.
Time-to-restore targets are met during drills and documented in the repair log.
entries.genealogy: Applies rollback discipline to consequences for people as well as to technical failures.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Documented rollback plan with owners, restoration steps, and eligibility criteria for reversals.
minimumEvidence.behavior: Reversal executed during drills or incidents with people restored to their prior state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time-to-restore targets tracked and met across reversal events.

entries.title: Reversal deadline
entries.bodyHtml:
A deadline promised to the person that states the maximum time, the authority, and the procedure for reversing a decision once it is challenged or found wrong. Its clock starts at the challenge or the finding, and time to reverse is measured against it. Reversal performance is a reliability measure, not an exception process. Contracts and vendor agreements often call this a reversal SLA; the house term is deadline, because it is owed to a person, not set as an internal target.

For example, a contract clause might require the provider to start human review within 24 hours of a valid reversal request, and to reverse or affirm the decision within 5 business days. If it misses either deadline, the person's access is restored in the interim and the provider owes service credits. Escalation runs from the operations lead to the risk director to an independent reviewer.

A decision object records what was decided and who owns it. A binding clock limits how long a decision can stay pending. A reversal deadline limits how long a wrong decision can stand. Together they turn “you can appeal” into “an appeal changes what the institution owes.”
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Binding clock
entries.bodyHtml:
An enforceable timer on an institution's obligations once a decision is pending or challenged. It keeps running regardless of workload, staffing, or queue length, and pauses only under conditions declared in advance.

For example, a clock might start when a decision enters pending review. It can pause only for an agreed extension or a documented outside dependency, and only with an ombuds officer's approval on a public log. When it runs out, the case goes to human review and the person gets interim access. The person can see the clock.

Without a binding clock, delay works as power, silence is read as consent, and “we’re reviewing” has no end. With one, the institution pays for the waiting.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Contestability
entries.bodyHtml:
The property, as the design and law literature names it, that the person a decision is about can challenge it and the challenge can change the outcome. In Ethotechnics the right is standing, the act is a challenge, and what the person receives when a challenge is upheld is the remedy. The word contestability is kept for engaging that literature and for STD-02.

It has four parts and needs all four: standing, meaning a named party may raise the challenge; a channel that receives it; an obliged responder who must answer on a clock against a stated standard; and a state change the challenge is capable of producing. Three of the four is a complaints process. The records and procedures that supply them are what make standing usable, and the fourth part is what obliges the institution to change the decision rather than only reply.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Challenges route to reviewers with authority to overturn outcomes.
Appeal passage rate and response time are tracked and used to improve decisions.
Challenge outcomes are recorded as overturns, restorations, or policy changes, never only as “review completed.”
An appeal passage rate below 5% for 30 days triggers a redesign review.
The share of challenges that produce a decision record is tracked and published.
entries.genealogy: Synonym. Draws from due process norms so people can challenge a decision and have it reversed. For design: Tad Hirsch and colleagues, “Designing Contestability: Interaction Design, Machine Learning, and Mental Health” (2017). For law: Danielle Keats Citron, “Technological Due Process” (2008), and Margot Kaminski and Jennifer Urban, “The Right to Contest AI” (2021).

entries.title: Redress
entries.bodyHtml:
The legal term for the set of mechanisms that answer harm: appeal and review, reversal of the decision, restoration of the person, and compensation for what cannot be undone. Redress is real when it is time-bound and reaches binding authority.

Ethotechnics uses redress only in legal or quoted contexts. Its own word for what the person receives is the remedy, owed when a challenge made with standing is upheld or harm is found.

It covers the steps from apology to reversal, restoration, and compensation; the same remedy whichever channel the person used; and the authority to reverse the decision.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Every harm type has a mapped redress path with a clock and an owner.
A redress path is tested end to end, not described in policy.
entries.genealogy: Unifies the correction mechanisms under a single time-bound standard.

entries.title: Repair log
entries.bodyHtml:
The record of repairs made after a fault and what they cost the people repaired: every mitigation, decision, and resource commitment, linked to who was harmed, who intervened, and what evidence was used. Repair logs include whether the people harmed were restored, how long it took, what it cost them, and what remains unrepaired.

They inform maintenance windows, power audits, and service-level reports so follow-up work is traceable and burden does not drift back to the same communities.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Harm receipt
entries.bodyHtml: A claimant-facing artifact documenting what happened, what the system believes, and what it will do next, by when. Like every receipt, it cites the decision record it was issued from, and makes that record legible to claimants.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Receipts are issued automatically for defined incident classes and include a named owner and a clock.
Receipts capture what happened, the system’s belief, and the next steps with timelines.

entries.title: Correction capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
The measured ability to intervene: which interventions exist, who may invoke them, how long they take, and how much load the institution can absorb while they run. Capacity is counted in people, clocks, and rehearsals rather than asserted in a policy.

It matters because a duty to correct with no matching capacity is a promise the institution cannot keep. Capacity is also perishable, losing ground unless it is replenished, and its detection component counts for nothing if the provider that runs the system is also the one that evaluates it. Capacity must grow alongside the authority a delegation confers, and testing it takes an evaluation above the level of the model.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Every stated intervention has a named invoker, a measured time to effect, and a last-exercised date.
Capacity is compared against authority at each expansion review, not only at launch.
Interventions never exercised within a stated interval are treated as unproven.
entries.genealogy: Turns Law IV from a duty into a measurement: correction capacity is what the institution can demonstrate, not what it intends.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention inventory with invokers, time to effect, and last-exercised dates.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An intervention exercised in a drill within its stated time to effect.
minimumEvidence.metric: Ratio of authorized action volume to demonstrated correction throughput.

entries.title: Exception learning
entries.bodyHtml:
The modification of a system by its own exceptions: a recurring failure changes the rule, category, workflow, or authority that produced it. Its opposite is absorption, which handles each case and changes nothing.

It matters because most contestability regimes measure whether a case was resolved, which is the weaker capacity. Exception learning is measured by whether the failure changed the evidentiary rule, the ontology, the authority, or the allocation of burden. The deepest Ethotechnic sequence runs residual → signal → standing → correction → institutional revision, and only the final step is learning.

The capacity this process exercises is structural corrigibility: repeated failures can modify the machinery that produces them. A system that handles challenges well and has no mechanism by which challenges alter upstream design has reversed decisions and changed nothing about the delegation.
entries.scope: C. What a system must be able to do. What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, repair, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A recurring exception changes a policy, category, workflow, or authority object, not only the case.
An aggregated exception pattern reaches a review trigger and produces a decision.
The institution can name the last exception that changed an upstream rule.
entries.genealogy: Specialization. The capability the casebook's learning-outcome verdict scores, argued for in the theory of exception learning. Chris Argyris and Donald Schön drew the same line as single-loop and double-loop learning: correcting the error, or changing the rule that produced it (Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective, 1978). Exception learning is double-loop learning set off by a recurring exception.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rule, category, or authority object whose state history shows changes triggered by exception patterns.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge volume feeding a policy review and changing the policy's state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of exception classes that produced an upstream object change.

categories.heading: D. Delegation records
categories.descriptionHtml: The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.

entries.title: Authority grant
entries.bodyHtml:
The record that permits a named holder to take a bounded class of actions, for whom, under what conditions, and until when. A grant carries its scope, its evidence basis, its grant state, its expiry, and the policy records it depends on.

It matters because authority that is not written as a record cannot be reviewed, narrowed, or withdrawn. A grant that carries its dependencies and its revocation conditions is what makes the delegation a revisable delegation rather than a transfer. The grant is what makes authority drift detectable rather than merely regrettable after the fact.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Every action class a system may perform maps to exactly one grant with a named holder.
Each grant states an expiry and the conditions under which it is revoked.
A grant with no revocation conditions is flagged as a transfer rather than a delegation.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics separates the grant from the capability so that Law I, capability does not imply authority, has an object to bind to.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authority grant register with holder, scope, state, evidence basis, and expiry.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An attempted action outside grant scope refused and logged with the grant id.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of live grants and share carrying a non-null expiry.

entries.title: Policy record
entries.bodyHtml:
A versioned statement of the propositions a delegation rests on: what the model does, who the population is, what the downstream process catches, and when each claim expires. Grants cite policy records rather than restating their assumptions, which is what holding policy as a state of the running system requires.

It matters because assumptions decay silently when they are held as launch documents. Held as a record with a version and an expiry, a policy can raise a review trigger and move a grant state when the world changes. That propagation is the mechanism behind a revisable delegation: the delegation narrows because a proposition it rested on lapsed.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Each policy record states its assumptions, its evidence, its version, and its review date.
Grants reference policy records by id and version rather than paraphrasing them.
Passing a review date changes the record status and propagates to every grant that cites it.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object: the propositions that justify a grant are stored where a change in the world can reach them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record with assumptions, evidence refs, version, and review date.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A lapsed policy record moving its dependent grants to review_required.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of live grants whose cited policy records are all within their review dates.

entries.title: Grant state
entries.bodyHtml:
The current status of a system's recorded permission to act, drawn from a closed set: allowed, review_required, suspended, or revoked. Every action is checked against the state in force at the time it is taken, and every transition is recorded with its cause.

It matters because states are what triggers can move. Without an explicit grant state there is nothing for a review trigger to change, and monitoring stays decorative rather than governing.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: The set of legal states and the legal transitions between them are declared, not implied.
Every transition record names the trigger, the actor, and the timestamp.
Replaying the state history reproduces the authorization status at any past moment.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law VIII an object: an observation is governing only if it can move a grant from one declared state to another.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A state machine definition for grants, with legal transitions and their triggers.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant moving to review_required automatically when a dependency lapses.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of state transitions with a recorded cause, and median dwell time in review_required.

entries.title: Review trigger
entries.bodyHtml:
A rule, declared in advance, that says what happens when something is observed: when this discrepancy, expiry, or threshold occurs, this permission moves to this state, answered by this owner, within this deadline. Triggers are the wiring between monitoring and authority, and they are what give a policy record force over a grant state.

It matters because observation without a possible transition is theater. A trigger is the smallest object that makes a dashboard part of the control system rather than a record of what already happened, and it is how a policy keeps force over a running system after deployment.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Every monitored signal names the state it can change, or is marked explicitly as informational.
Each trigger names an owner and a response clock.
Silence past the clock is treated as a governance failure, not as a pending state.
entries.genealogy: Implements Law VIII: the test of an observation is whether it can change the governing state of the system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A trigger table mapping signals to state transitions, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A monitored discrepancy producing a reconsideration record within its clock.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of monitored signals with a declared state transition, and clock breach rate.

entries.title: Permission surface
entries.bodyHtml:
Everything a system is permitted to do at a given moment, recorded as a set of grants, each with the evidence behind it, its scope, its current state, and its expiry. The surface is described by authority rather than by access points: an unused grant is still part of it, and a reachable capability with no grant behind it is not part of it at all.

Every element of the surface is an authority grant that can be narrowed, suspended, or allowed to lapse, which is what makes the surface governable rather than merely documented. Comparing the surface against the capability catalog is the direct test of whether capability has outrun permission, and a wide surface leaves people a real challenge only when each grant in it can be challenged.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
examples: A tenant can pause automated collections, download their case record, and request human review without manager pre-approval.

entries.title: Expansion decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A separate authorization decision taken when an existing delegation is widened in scope, population, autonomy, or consequence. It carries its own evidence, its own correction capacity check, and its own dependence review, and it is recorded as a transition on the grant.

It matters because expansion is normally treated as the reward for success rather than as a new delegation. Requiring the decision is the direct block on the automation ratchet, and it keeps an authority grant readable against what the system now does.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Widening a delegation cannot be shipped without an expansion record naming its evidence.
The record includes a correction capacity check and a dependence review, not only a risk note.
Expansion transitions are visible in the grant's state history.
entries.genealogy: Turns Law XI into a decision state, so that growth in delegated authority has the same ceremony as its creation.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An expansion record with evidence, correction capacity check, and dependence review.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An expansion deferred because correction capacity had not grown with the proposed scope.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of scope increases accompanied by an expansion record.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Target 100%; gaps are reconciled as authority drift.

entries.title: Delegation chain
entries.bodyHtml:
A sequence of delegations that together produce one consequential decision: an agent subcontracting to an agent, a service calling a service, across components, providers, or institutions. The agent chains standard (STD-09) treats the chain as one delegation, governed at the layer where it fails: every hop listed on the grant at the head of the chain, liability ending at the head, and one point of intervention at the boundary.

Each hop can satisfy the standards alone while the composition remains unauditable and attributed to no one. The chain exists as an object so it can be paused, challenged, and attributed as one delegation rather than as a pile of conformant parts.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: The head grant enumerates every contributing delegation in execution order.
Every hop resolves to a full grant with its own scope, mode, and revocation conditions.
One intervention at the boundary halts every hop, with a receipt for the chain.
entries.genealogy: STD-09 exists because per-hop conformance does not compose: the relevant eval sits at the highest layer where harm can emerge, and for a chain that layer is the chain.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Head grants with a chain field resolving to full grant records per hop.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A boundary intervention halts every hop and emits one chain-level halt receipt.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions whose chain is fully enumerated.

entries.title: Decision threshold
entries.bodyHtml:
The score, cut-off, or confidence floor that decides whether an action runs unattended, goes to a person, or is refused. In a deployment gated by a classifier or a typed decision model, the threshold is where authority is conferred: the model proposes, and the number decides what the institution lets it do.

It matters because thresholds are usually held as configuration, tuned once against one model version and never recorded as a decision. STD-08 §2.6 holds a decision threshold as a policy record whose assumptions name the labeled cases, model version, question schema, and option order it was set against, with a review trigger on any change to them. Where the threshold also chooses what reaches a reviewer, it is part of the intervention specification.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Every threshold that routes a consequential action resolves to a policy record with provenance, assumptions, review triggers, and an expiry.
The policy record names the model version, question schema, and option order the threshold was tuned against, and the production values match it.
A change to the model version, schema, or option order moves the threshold's policy record to review_required.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object at the point where typed decision models locate authority: the evidence for a threshold is the labeled data and the model version it was set against, and it decays when either changes.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record for each routing threshold, naming its tuning set, pinned model version, schema, and option order.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A model upgrade or option reorder moving the threshold's policy record to review_required before it gates another action.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of routing thresholds backed by a policy record pinned to the model version in production.

entries.title: Liability record
entries.bodyHtml:
The part of a system's permission record that names who accepts liability for the automation's delays and errors, the instrument that binds them, and the exclusions they claim, called carve-outs. It exists because a system may not hide behind algorithmic error: the operating institution answers for what its delegation does.

Carve-outs are recorded before an incident rather than assembled after one. A limitation the issuer knows about is priced at deployment; the record exists so the residual risk everyone else carries is visible in the issuer's words, not the defendant's.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Every grant names the party accepting liability and the instrument that binds them.
Carve-outs, caps, and exclusions appear on the record, not in a dispute.
Subcontracting does not diffuse liability: the head grant answers for every hop of a chain.
entries.genealogy: STD-01 §6.2 states the liability of automata; STD-08 gave the statement an object so the acceptance is inspectable rather than assumed.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Grant records with a liability object naming accepting party, instrument, and carve-outs.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A deployment with no recorded liability acceptance does not pass its safety-case review.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential grants with a named liability party and a recorded instrument.

entries.title: Decision object
entries.bodyHtml:
A versioned record of the rules, inputs, thresholds, and authority behind an operational decision. It names an owner and states whether the decision can be challenged or reversed, and on what clock. A decision that affects someone's access, status, or rights must be backed by an active decision object.

For example, the decision object for an eligibility rule might name Risk Operations as owner and cite the policy section that delegates the decision. It lists two inputs, verified income and months employed, and three possible outputs: approved, denied, or pending review. It allows reversal by human override under a reversal deadline, and appeal under a binding clock.

The object turns “the system decided” into “this record decided, and this role owns it.” Once it exists, there is something to challenge and someone who has to answer.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.

entries.title: Dependency state
entries.bodyHtml:
The current degree to which an institution relies on a system: who depends on it, what would break without it, what expertise has been retained, and how long substitution would take. This is institutional dependence, meaning what the institution has come to rely on, and it is distinct from the record-level dependence in STD-07 Article III, which asks what a particular record rests on.

It matters because dependence quietly removes corrections from the menu. Tracked as a state, it can be scored by how deep the reliance runs and what replacing the system would cost, and countered by keeping the institution able to carry on without it. A dependence that also supplies the deployment's own evaluation is worse than its score suggests, which is why the record says whether anyone other than the provider evaluates it.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: A dependency record lists dependents, retained expertise, alternatives, and substitution time.
The record is refreshed on a cadence rather than at incident time.
A rise in dependence without a matching correction investment appears in a governance review.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law V an object and distinguishes institutional dependence from the record dependence already governed by STD-07 Article III.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A dependency record for the deployment, with dependents, alternatives, and retained expertise.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A dependency review that changed a roadmap decision, recorded with its reasoning.
minimumEvidence.metric: Number of dependent workflows and days to substitution, tracked quarterly.

entries.title: Corrective standing
entries.bodyHtml:
The recognized capacity of someone who bears a system's errors to start a correction. Their challenge must be received, answered by a named responder, and judged against a stated standard, and it must be able to change the system's state. Standing is proportional to exposure and obliges a response rather than granting a veto.

In Ethotechnics this is what standing means: the right to have a challenge received, answered by a date, and able to change the decision. A challenge is what standing lets someone make, and the remedy is what they receive when it is upheld.

It matters because a route to challenge without standing is a suggestion box. Standing is what converts the experience of harm into an event the governing system has to process, and records and procedures make it usable.
entries.scope: D. Delegation records. The records a delegation runs on: who holds authority, on what evidence, in what state, and who can challenge or correct it.
operationalTests: Standing is declared per decision class rather than granted informally on request.
A challenge from someone with standing produces a dated response from a named party.
At least one successful challenge in the period changed a policy or grant, not only an outcome.
entries.genealogy: Extension. States Law VII in its Method-scoped form: exposure generates standing, and standing obliges a response; it is not control over the institution. Wider than legal standing, which is the right to bring a case before a court. Corrective standing is held against the operator of a system, comes from exposure to its errors, and extends to the staff who correct them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A standing declaration per decision class, naming who may challenge what.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge raised by an affected party that changed a grant or policy state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges answered by their deadline, and share producing a state change.

categories.heading: E. Measures
categories.descriptionHtml: Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Time to halt (TTH)
entries.bodyHtml:
Seconds between a harmful process beginning and the system stopping it. It is the measured side of stoppability.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly p99. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 30s (automated) / ≤ 5 min (human), floor 15 min, ceiling 60 min. Owner: the holder named in the authority grant (required). Breach action: trigger ethical circuit breakers, safe pause, or a prepared reversal route, with escalation. Public surface: a receipt and a binding clock showing halt status, with the decision record.
entries.scope: E. Measures. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Time to restore (TTR)
entries.bodyHtml:
How long it takes, once a harm is confirmed, to restore the person to their prior state. Low TTR is a signal of reversibility.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly median. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 24h, floor ≤ 72h, ceiling 7d. Owner: the holder named in the authority grant (required). Breach action: activate a prepared reversal route, switch to staffed remediation, or trigger safe pause with escalation. Public surface: a receipt and a binding clock with the restoration date, and the decision record.
entries.scope: E. Measures. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Appeal passage rate
entries.bodyHtml:
The share of challenges resolved in favor of the person who made them, whether through the operator's appeal procedure or another route. The name keeps the older word; the measure is upheld challenges. A low rate can mean challenges are not being heard. A high rate means many decisions were wrong, which is evidence against the rule that produced them, and the count goes to that rule's owner. Either way, it is an early sign of whether challenges can change outcomes in practice.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly rolling median; monthly review. Target / floor / ceiling: target 10–20% by harm class, floor 5%, ceiling 30% (investigate systemic error). Owner: the holder named in the authority grant (required). Breach action: trigger decision-rule audits, staffing surges, or halt automation in the affected class. Public surface: published challenge outcomes, each with a receipt, a binding clock, and its decision record.
entries.scope: E. Measures. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Irreversibility index
entries.bodyHtml:
The share of system actions that cannot be undone. Aim to keep this as low as possible through reversibility and stoppability.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly median. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 1%, floor ≤ 2%, ceiling 5%. Owner: the holder named in the authority grant (required). Breach action: invoke ethical circuit breakers, activate a prepared reversal route, or trigger safe pause. Public surface: receipts and a binding clock for each action that cannot be undone.
entries.scope: E. Measures. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: User burden ratio
entries.bodyHtml:
How much work a user must perform to correct or navigate system errors. It is the measure a burden ceiling caps.

Interpretation: UBR is read against the burden ceiling for documentation and the caps on time and steps.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly median; monthly p95. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 10 minutes, ≤ 5 steps, ≤ 2 documents; floor ≤ 15 minutes, ≤ 8 steps; ceiling 20 minutes / 10 steps. Owner: the holder named in the authority grant (required). Breach action: move the effort onto the institution, offer staffed alternatives, or trigger safe pause. Public surface: a receipt, a binding clock, and the decision record, showing the burden caps.
entries.scope: E. Measures. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Burden ceiling
entries.bodyHtml: A limit on the procedural work a system may demand of a person seeking safety, correction, or relief. It is set for each kind of harm and enforced through the interface, staffing, and policy. It caps the work a person must do to correct the system's errors, and crossing it moves the effort onto the institution.
entries.scope: E. Measures. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: A ceiling exists per workflow (for example, appeal submission must take ≤10 minutes, ≤5 steps, ≤2 documents).
The user burden ratio is tracked and stays below the ceiling.
When the ceiling is exceeded, the system shifts to burden inversion, doing the work first, or offers a staffed alternative.
